comment.value: The paper presents a dataset and a study to compare and benchmark the performance of 3D shape inference between humans and some current large vision models. The reviewers agree that the dataset is reasonably extensive and diverse (some suggestions for further extensions have been discussed with the authors) and has the potential to be used by the research community when released with all the accompanying data, including human behavioral data and code for evaluation metrics. The reviewers also appreciate the proposed evaluation metrics, which reveal discrepancies between human performance and current large vision models and motivate future research efforts. There is also agreement among the reviewers that the paper is clearly written and well-structured. Some of the weaknesses have been discussed during the rebuttal phase, and some improvements will be included in the revised version of the paper. Overall, there is a consensus to accept the paper, and the AC agrees with the recommendation.

Thank anthors for the response and for addressing the concerns raised by me and other reviewers. I look forward to the authors adding the discussion about more the design and evaluation of more sophisticated readout methods as future direction.

Thank you for your positive feedback and for recognizing the importance of our work for the community. We appreciate your questions about the dataset and its potential applications.

1. Dataset open-sourcing: We plan to open-source the entire dataset upon publication of the paper. This will include: a) All image triplets b) Human behavioral data (choices, reaction times, and eye-tracking) c) Evaluation metrics and scripts d) Detailed documentation for dataset usage and replication of our experiments We will make this available through a public repository, likely on GitHub, with accompanying documentation.
2. Handling 3D assets with artifacts or deformations: This is an excellent question about the robustness of our benchmark. Currently, our dataset focuses on clean, well-formed 3D models. However, your question highlights an important area for future work. Any suggestions you have in this area would be greatly appreciated! 
3. Semantic misalignment: Thank you for raising this point. While our current benchmark does not explicitly address semantic misalignment, we agree that this is an important aspect of 3D understanding. We will include this as a potential direction for future work, discussing how our benchmark could be extended to incorporate semantic aspects of 3D shapes.

Thank you for your valuable feedback, which has helped us identify important areas for discussion and future research directions.

We will expand our discussion to include these potential applications in the paper.
2. Data and benchmark release: We plan to release all data and benchmark materials upon publication of the paper. This will include the image triplets, human behavioral data (choices, reaction times, and eye-tracking), and evaluation metrics, along with detailed documentation to facilitate their use by the research community.

rebuttal.value:
Thank you for your positive evaluation of our paper and for recognizing the significance of our work. We appreciate your detailed comments and suggestions for improvement.

1. Dataset quality and diversity: We acknowledge your concern about the quality and diversity of our dataset. Your suggestion to incorporate higher-fidelity stimulus sets, such as those from Objaverse, is excellent and would allow us to expand on the 3D probing abilities that our inaugural dataset establishes. We hope that in future iterations of this benchmark, as we expand the number of images for better coverage of relevant objects, we will be able to incorporate higher-quality 3D objects, including those from objaverse. Unfortunately, due to the amount of time required to construct and collect additional datasets, we will not be able to include this expansion in the current submission. 
2. Evaluation metrics: We agree that our current evaluation metrics have limitations, especially for powerful visual models like DINOv2. We believe that our linear probes are a suitable starting point, but in no way reflect the upper bound of what models such as DINOv2 are capable of. Indeed, we hope that by making this benchmark available to the community that researchers are able to design and evaluate more powerful readout methods; in our minds, this is perhaps the most promising future research direction. We plan to modify our conclusion to make this clear, and to discuss how more sophisticated evaluation methods could potentially reveal deeper insights into these models' attention mechanisms.
3. Minor corrections: Thank you for pointing out the typo on line 206. We will correct this and carefully review the manuscript for any other minor errors.

We appreciate your thorough review and confidence in our work. Your feedback will help us improve the paper's overall quality and impact.

Thank you for your positive feedback and insightful comments. We appreciate your recognition of our paper's contribution and the extensive experiments conducted.

1. DINOv2 performance: You raise an excellent point about DINOv2's performance in distinguishing low similarity objects. We agree that the contrastive learning setup likely contributes to this behavior. We will expand our discussion to explore this connection more thoroughly, highlighting how the model's training objective aligns with our task in beneficial and destructive ways. 
2. Augmentations: Your suggestion to run multiple trials with different augmentations is intriguing. We agree that this could provide valuable insights into model behavior and potentially improve performance, though it is not obvious to us how to conduct the comparison between human reaction time to model augmentations—any suggestions here would be greatly appreciated! Regardless, we will include this as a future research direction in our discussion, emphasizing the potential for studying the trade-off between reaction time and accuracy in models, similar to humans.
3. Golden standard for 3D understanding: We appreciate you raising this point. We believe that this is such an important question we should engage with it in depth in our introduction. To reiterate the general point we made in the general response: While we do not know what the gold standard for evaluating the 3D abilities of vision models should be, we believe that focusing on model abilities provides a useful framework for engaging with this problem. The passage we’ve included in the general response is a good summary of our changes, but let us know if you’d like us to share the complete intro. 


Thank you for your valuable feedback! Your suggestions and comments about how the contrastive learning objective in DINOv2 are especially helpful. We look forward to using these suggestions to improve our analysis.

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive feedback on our paper. We are pleased that they recognize the significance of our benchmark for evaluating the alignment between human behavior and vision models on 3D visual understanding. In particular, we are glad that they found that:

- Our benchmark contains an extensive, diverse, and informative set of human behavioral measures. [TLqL, H8cM, 9pbj]
- Our evaluation metrics are thoughtfully designed to show the limitations of current large vision models and motivate further modeling efforts. [TLqL, qBmW]
- Our manuscript is well-written and easy to follow. [qBmW, TLqL, 9pbj]

We outline some common concerns in this global response, and respond to individual reviews under the corresponding thread. Additionally, we highlight changes we intend to make to our manuscript in the global and individual responses where appropriate. 
Data availability.

There was a common interest that we make all data and evaluation code available. \textbf{We agree that this is a critical aspect of our work and upon publication will open-source all data, including the image triplets, human behavioral data, and code for evaluation metrics.}This will include detailed documentation to facilitate its use by the research community. We hope that this will enable the community to improve on our initial model evaluations and close the gap between humans and vision models! 

Proposed changes to the introduction: 

Reviewer qBmW raised a question we would like to engage with in the introduction more fully: “What is the golden standard for 3d understanding?” In addition to providing a formal comparison between humans and vision models, we believe that our benchmark proposes a relatively novel evaluation framework: the experiments we adopt from the cognitive sciences probe 3D visual abilities without making strong assumptions about how this information should be represented (e.g., pointclouds, depth maps). While we do not know what the gold standard for evaluating the 3D abilities of vision models should be, we believe that this transition from representations to abilities provides a useful framework for engaging with this problem.

Below we outline some of the changes we would like to make to the introduction, opening with:  

> Do computer vision models represent the 3D structure of objects? Answering this question is more difficult than it might appear. Many tasks that seem to require explicit 3D representations can be performed directly from 2D visual features. Depth estimation, for example, is commonly used to evaluate a model's 3D 'awareness' [1], even though depth can be predicted using cues such as texture gradients [2], relative size [3], shading [4], and camera blur [5]. '3D understanding' may simply be a composite of such 2D features  (e.g., the Aspect Graph model [6]), or it might require representations not directly accessible in these lower-level visual statistics [7]. As large-scale vision models become more capable, these questions take on new implications. What methods might help us understand how vision models represent objects?

> The cognitive sciences have grappled with questions about 3D perception for decades. To understand human visual abilities, … 

and continuing on to outline the benefits of our approach: 

> Two aspects of these experiments are especially relevant for evaluating contemporary vision models. First, these tasks are  agnostic as to how shape information is represented, focusing instead on visual abilities. This is in contrast to current computer vision methods which make strong assumptions about how 3D representations are formatted (e.g., depth, point clouds). Second, human-model alignment provides a better guarantee that model performance might relate to more general notions of '3D understanding'. That is, models that best predict human behaviors are those models most likely to exhibit similar choice behaviors in related tasks [8]. This requires going beyond determining if models achieve human-level performance (i.e., average accuracy) and evaluating whether models exhibit human-like performance (e.g., correlated choice behaviors).

Summary

We are grateful for all the supportive feedback and suggestions, and invite the reviewers to engage in the following discussion period to further strengthen our benchmarking and analyses. We look forward to the improved version of our manuscript, and to releasing this dataset to the community! 

References

[1] El Banani, Mohamed, et al. "Probing the 3d awareness of visual foundation models." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF CVPR 2024.

[2] Malik, Jitendra, and Ruth Rosenholtz. "Computing local surface orientation and shape from texture for curved surfaces." IJCV 23.2 (1997): 149-168.

[3] Cutting, James E., and Peter M. Vishton. "Perceiving layout and knowing distances: The integration, relative potency, and contextual use of different information about depth." Perception of space and motion. Academic Press, 1995. 69-117.

[4] Ramachandran, Vilayanur S. "Perception of shape from shading." Nature 331.6152 (1988): 163-166.

[5] Mather, George. "Image blur as a pictorial depth cue." Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series B: Biological Sciences 263.1367 (1996): 169-172.

[6] Koenderink, Jan J., and Andrea J. Van Doorn. "The internal representation of solid shape with respect to vision." Biological cybernetics 32.4 (1979): 211-216.

[7] Marr, David. Vision: A computational investigation into the human representation and processing of visual information. MIT press, 2010.

[8] Cao, Rosa, and Daniel Yamins. "Explanatory models in neuroscience, Part 1: Taking mechanistic abstraction seriously." Cognitive Systems Research (2024): 101244.

title.value: An interesting study for evaluating the 3D understanding of vision models comparing with human behavioral data

summary_and_contributions.value: The authors propose a benchmark to evaluate the alignment between human behavior and vision models on 3D visual understanding. For this, they prepared an experimental setup for zero-shot visual inferences about object shape: given three images, participants identify which contain the same/different objects, in spite of considerable viewpoint variation. Authors constructed over 2000 unique image triplets and collected 35K trials of human behavioral data from over 500 participants. Self-supervised models such as (contrastive) DINOv2 and masked autoencoding (MAE), CLIP are evaluated for the same task. The paper shows several insights about underlying similarities/dissimilarities between human and model choice behaviors. Nonetheless, humans outperform all models by a wide margin.

review.value:
- It is an noteworthy observation that dinov2 works well with distinguishing low similarity objects but fails in high similarity object settings. Why DINOv2 outperforms MAE and CLIP? Can we attribute this to the contrastive learning setup where they are leant to contrast dissimilar visuals and match similar visuals. This seems to be quite similar to the proposed behavior task. 

- Section 3.4 shows that the same trials that dinov2 models perform poorly on are the very trials that humans allocate more time to process. What would happen if we run multiple trails for models with different augmentations (eg. rotated image, high resolution) of visual data? As humans, we too imagine different augmentations of the visual image to find and distinguish the matches. This is evident from the study that humans take more reaction times for challenging trails. We can also study the trade-off between reaction time and accuracy for models similar to humans.

- DINOv2 works as good as humans in "lowsim" settings as in Figure 7. I would argue that dinov2 is not encouraged to learn to contrast between high similarity object features and it has looked less of textureless data. With the above two, dinov2 could potentially become competitive with humans on "highsim" evaluation as well. Will that indicate that dinov2 are good at 3D understanding? What is the golden standard for 3d understanding?

strengths.value:
- The paper is well written and easy to follow

- Extensive experiments and analysis with graphical plots look impressive. 

- The work shows the limitations of the current large visual foundational models. This can help in modelling visual models to have a better 3D understanding.

title.value: A novel benchmark to evaluate vision models against human behavior on 3D shape inference

summary_and_contributions.value:
The paper introduced a benchmark to evaluate how human observers and vision models perform on one specific task of 3D shape inference, i.e, picking out the different shape from a triplet. 

Contributions
The paper introduced a benchmark to evaluate how human observers and vision models perform on one specific task of 3D shape inference, i.e, picking out the different shape from a triplet. 

Contributions
* A dataset consists of 2000 unique image triplets from 4 stimulus sets.
* 35K trials of behavior data from over 500 participants are collected, and a series of granular evaluation metrics using choice, reaction time and eye-tracking measurements are defined.
* 3 popular vision models, DINOv2, MAE, and CLIP are evaluated on 3 metrics: distance metrics, standard linear probe, and a lightweight linear classification.
* Demonstrated a clear relationship between human and model behaviors.
* Discovered that human gaze patterns are reliable but not predicted by model self-attention.

review.value: The paper is well written. I consider the work significant as through thoughtful design of evaluation metrics and experiments, it illuminates how popular vision models compare with human behavior in the task of 3D understanding. I will list the pros and cons in the following sections.

strengths.value:
* The paper provides a novel benchmark to evaluate how vision models compare to human behaviors on a 3D shape inference task. 
* The collection of human behavior data, especially the granular evaluation metrics, is quite an effort. Such data illustrate the correlation and subtle differences between human and model behaviors.
* The evaluation metrics and experiments are thoughtfully designed.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
* the dataset size and diversity could be improved. The quality (realism) of the 3D models used are on the fairly low end, which may potentially introduce unintended bias in the human response. Given the rise of higher quality 3D datasets, such as Objaverse, the author could consider constructing some additional higher fidelity stimulus sets.
* As acknowledged by the authors, the model 3 evaluation metrics explored in the paper are limited. Powerful visual representations such as DINOv2 would probably benefit from stronger models which could close the gap between human and model performance. In addition, they may reveal deeper insight into these models’ attention mechanisms.

correctness.value: The dataset construction, human data collection, and experiment design seems to be correct.

clarity.value: The paper is well-written with a few minor exceptions, e.g. line 206: t0test.

relation_to_prior_work.value: The reference seems to be adequate and the relevance to the prior work is clearly stated. However, I have to admit that I’m not familiar with the human vision study literature.

ethics.value: I have no ethics concerns with this work.

summary_and_contributions.value: The research introduces a novel benchmark aimed at assessing the alignment between human observers and vision models in terms of 3D shape inference. This benchmark includes a diverse set of images, both common objects and abstract shapes, presented in various viewpoints, lighting conditions, and backgrounds. Over 500 participants contributed to the collection of 35,000 trials, which were analyzed using choice behavior, reaction time, and eye-tracking data. The study evaluates models trained with contrastive learning (DINOv2), masked autoencoding (MAE), and language-image pretraining (CLIP). Despite some similarities in choice behavior, humans significantly outperform all models tested.

review.value:
- The dataset used in the study is extensive and diverse, featuring over 2000 unique image triplets with variations in viewpoint, lighting, and background. And when and in what way do the authors plan to open source the dataset?
- Can this benchmark handle 3d assets that face artifacts or have deformations (e.g., semantic misalignment)?
- All in all it's good work and very important for the community, if this data can be open sourced as expected

title.value: Evaluating Multiview Object Consistency in Humans and Image Models

TLDR.value: A benchmark to evaluate the alignment between vision models and human 3D perception

abstract.value: We introduce a benchmark to directly evaluate the alignment between human observers and vision models on a 3D shape inference task. We leverage an experimental design from the cognitive sciences: given a set of images, participants identify which contain the same/different objects, despite considerable viewpoint variation. We draw from a diverse range of images that include common objects (e.g., chairs) as well as abstract shapes (i.e., procedurally generated 'nonsense' objects). After constructing over 2000 unique image sets, we administer these tasks to human participants, collecting 35K trials of behavioral data from over 500 participants. This includes explicit choice behaviors as well as intermediate measures, such as reaction time and gaze data. We then evaluate the performance of common vision models (e.g., DINOv2, MAE, CLIP). We find that humans outperform all models by a wide margin. Using a multi-scale evaluation approach, we identify underlying similarities and differences between models and humans: while human-model performance is correlated, humans allocate more time/processing on challenging trials. All images, data, and code can be accessed via our project page.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
